This 70-page annual financial report for Laurentian University’s fiscal year ended April 30, 2021 records the university’s finances during its Companies’ Creditors Arrangement Act (CCAA) restructuring. On February 1, 2021, the Ontario Superior Court placed Laurentian under CCAA protection and appointed Ernst & Young Inc. as monitor; the court approved Firm Capital Corporation debtor-in-possession financing initially capped at $25 million and later increased to $35 million. Laurentian closed 39 English-language and 27 French-language programs, began terminating its federated-university relationships, and negotiated workforce, compensation, pension and post-employment-benefit changes that management said would reduce operating expenses by $40 million annually, or 25%. The restructuring included $78.9 million in one-time costs, including $45.4 million in workforce adjustments, $24.7 million to terminate seven interest-rate swaps and $8.8 million in professional fees.

For 2020-21, revenue was $193.4 million, expenses were $260.1 million and the deficiency of revenue over expenses was $66.7 million; excluding restructuring costs, expenses fell 9.8% to $181.2 million while revenue declined 2.1%. Pandemic disruption reduced sales and services revenue from $11.6 million to $5.6 million, with residence occupancy averaging 40% versus more than 96% historically. At year-end, Laurentian reported $381.1 million of assets, $396.5 million of liabilities and negative net assets of $15.4 million; liabilities subject to compromise totaled $186.8 million, while creditors had asserted claims totaling $360.3 million. Cash and short-term investments were $37.0 million, largely reflecting DIP financing and spending controls, but operating cash flow was negative $75.1 million before the change in compromise liabilities, and the university’s existing $31 million of unsecured bank credit lines were unavailable.

Management disclosed significant uncertainty over Laurentian’s ability to continue as a going concern, dependent on restructuring and emergence from CCAA, alongside Ontario’s announced support of up to $35 million to refinance the DIP loan, $6 million in COVID funding and up to $22 million in enrolment and performance protection. KPMG LLP ultimately issued an unmodified opinion on the amended and restated statements, while drawing attention to the material going-concern uncertainty; the report was dated March 7, 2022, with an amendment dated April 22, 2022. The comparative 2020 figures and the 2021 statements were corrected after the CCAA-related review identified errors involving deferred contributions, pension and retiree benefits, endowment allocations, vacation pay and capital projects; the 2021 amendment changed revenue and expense classifications but did not affect assets, liabilities, net assets or cash flows.

Sales and services revenue fell from $11.6 million in the previous year to $5.6 million in 2020-21; average residence occupancy was 40%, compared with a historical average above 96% over the prior five years.

Fall 2020 student headcount was 9,323, up 4.2% from the previous year, but the University reported a 14% reduction in total fall 2021 enrolment after the fiscal year-end and anticipated another significant reduction in fall 2022.

Laurentian University's sales and services revenue fell to $5.6 million in 2020-21 from $11.6 million, primarily because pandemic restrictions disrupted on-campus activities; housing, food and parking accounted for 72% of the shortfall, and average residence occupancy fell to 40% from a historical average above 96%.

Laurentian University's total expenses were $260.1 million in 2020-21, including $78.9 million of CCAA-related restructuring costs; expenses excluding restructuring costs were $181.2 million, down $19.7 million from the prior year.

Laurentian University's salaries and benefits were $128.4 million in 2020-21, $6.4 million below the prior year; negotiated CCAA savings with the Laurentian University Staff Union and Laurentian University Faculty Association were expected to take effect in fiscal 2021-22.

Amendments to the Employees Retirement Plan took effect July 1, 2021, including a career-average earnings formula, removal of guaranteed post-retirement indexation, changes to early-retirement benefits and elimination of the ability to draw a pension while continuing to work.
Laurentian terminated its Retirees' Health and Benefit Plan and Supplemental Retirement Plan effective April 30, 2021.

Laurentian recognized $78.9 million of one-time CCAA restructuring expenses in 2020-21, comprising a $24.7 million loss from terminating interest-rate swaps, $45.4 million of workforce adjustment and termination costs, and $8.8 million of legal, monitor and consulting costs.
Laurentian's seven interest-rate swap agreements were terminated after the CCAA filing constituted an event of default, producing an immediate $24.7 million loss recorded as a restructuring cost.

Laurentian's historic federated relationships with Huntington University, University of Sudbury and Thorneloe University were terminated through a statutory mechanism approved in the CCAA proceeding and upheld by the Court of Appeal; payments to the federated universities were $7.7 million in 2020-21.

Laurentian reported a deferred-maintenance backlog estimated at $135.0 million; it invested $1.4 million in capital projects during 2020-21, primarily for critical maintenance, compared with $2.8 million in 2020.

Court-approved super-priority DIP financing provided by Firm Capital Corporation replaced Laurentian's unavailable bank credit lines; the facility initially permitted up to $25.0 million, was increased to $35.0 million near the end of fiscal 2020-21, and $10.0 million of the increased availability was drawn after year-end.

Laurentian ended fiscal 2020-21 with $37.0 million in cash and short-term investments, compared with $3.4 million the previous year; the increase was attributed principally to DIP financing and tighter spending controls.
Laurentian's $5.0 million Royal Bank unsecured line of credit and $26.0 million Desjardins unsecured line of credit were no longer available as of April 30, 2021.

Laurentian's liabilities subject to compromise totaled $186.8 million, including $11.3 million of accounts payable and accrued liabilities, $59.6 million of employee restructuring and termination costs, $1.3 million of short-term loans, $89.9 million of long-term debt and $24.7 million of interest-rate-swap termination obligations.

At April 30, 2021, Laurentian reported no long-term debt compared with $89.0 million in 2020 because CCAA-related defaults made the debt immediately due and the obligations were reclassified as liabilities subject to compromise.

At April 30, 2021, Laurentian included $10.8 million relating to the Retirees' Health and Benefit Plan and $3.2 million relating to the Supplemental Retirement Plan in liabilities subject to compromise; the Employees Retirement Plan's $12.3 million accrued-benefits liability was also reclassified into that category.
Laurentian reported a $15.4 million deficiency in net assets at the end of fiscal 2020-21, driven primarily by a $66.7 million deficiency of revenue over expenses.

Ontario announced support including $35.0 million to refinance Laurentian's DIP financing, an intended long-term loan upon a successful CCAA exit, up to $6.0 million in COVID funding, and up to $22.0 million in enrolment-corridor and performance protection.

Management acknowledged considerable material uncertainty about Laurentian's ability to continue as a going concern while stating that restructuring actions and Ontario's announced support would assist a successful CCAA exit.

KPMG LLP issued an unmodified audit opinion on Laurentian University of Sudbury's restated consolidated financial statements for the year ended April 30, 2021, prepared under Canadian accounting standards for not-for-profit organizations.
KPMG's report drew attention to a material uncertainty related to going concern because Laurentian obtained a CCAA stay on February 1, 2021, and the stay had been extended to May 31, 2022.

KPMG stated that Laurentian's financial statements originally reported on March 7, 2022 had been amended, with the amendment addressed in Note 27; the auditor's opinion was not modified in respect of the amendment.
KPMG reported that comparative information for the year ended April 30, 2020 had been restated and corrected, and stated that the adjustments were appropriate and properly applied.
The auditors' report is dated March 7, 2022, except for Note 27, which is dated April 22, 2022.

Y.summary:
Laurentian University’s 2020-21 annual financial report presents its amended, restated financial statements and the financial consequences of the university’s CCAA restructuring. For the year ended April 30, 2021, revenue was $193.4 million and expenses were $260.1 million, producing a $66.7 million deficiency that included $78.9 million in CCAA-related restructuring costs; net assets were negative $15.4 million, total liabilities were $396.5 million against $381.1 million of assets, and operating activities used $75.1 million in cash. The university had $37.0 million in cash and short-term investments at year-end, but its $186.8 million of recognized liabilities were subject to compromise, while creditors asserted claims totaling $360.3 million.

Laurentian sought CCAA protection on February 1, 2021, with Ernst & Young Inc. appointed monitor, and drew the full initial $25 million super-priority debtor-in-possession facility before it was increased to $35 million. The filing triggered defaults on debt and seven interest-rate swaps, producing a $24.7 million swap-termination loss; $89.9 million of long-term debt, employee-related obligations, termination costs and other claims were reclassified as subject to compromise. Restructuring included closing 39 English-language and 27 French-language programs, workforce and benefit changes, terminating retiree benefit plans and historic federated-university relationships, and was expected to reduce annual operating expenses by about $40 million.

The report highlights material uncertainty about Laurentian’s ability to continue as a going concern, driven by the CCAA proceedings, cash-flow and working-capital deficiencies and negative net assets. Ontario subsequently pledged to refinance the $35 million DIP loan, provide up to $6 million in COVID-19 funding and up to $22 million in enrolment-corridor and performance protection, subject to board renewal and a long-term strategic plan; the replacement facility was completed in January 2022. KPMG issued an unmodified opinion under Canadian accounting standards for not-for-profit organizations but emphasized that the statements had been amended and comparative figures restated after accounting errors and policy changes were identified.

Laurentian University’s Annual Financial Report for fiscal 2020-21 presents the university’s amended and restated consolidated financial statements and related disclosures amid its Companies’ Creditors Arrangement Act restructuring. For the year ended April 30, 2021, revenue fell to $193.4 million while expenses rose to $260.1 million, producing a $66.7 million deficiency and reducing net assets to a $15.4 million deficiency from $34.8 million of restated net assets the prior year. The deficit included $78.9 million of CCAA-related restructuring costs; excluding those costs, expenses were $181.2 million and the university reported an adjusted $12.2 million excess. Cash and short-term investments increased to $37.0 million, largely reflecting the $25 million debtor-in-possession facility drawn by year-end and later increased to $35 million, while $186.8 million of liabilities were classified as subject to compromise and creditors asserted claims totaling $360.3 million.

Laurentian entered CCAA protection on February 1, 2021 after years of operating deficits, with Ernst & Young Inc. appointed monitor. The restructuring included closing 39 English-language and 27 French-language programs, reducing faculty and staff, ending relationships with Thorneloe University, University of Sudbury and Huntington University, terminating retiree benefit plans, changing pension terms, and negotiating workforce and collective-agreement changes; the university said these measures reduced annual operating costs by about $40 million. Ontario later supported refinancing the DIP loan, offered up to $6 million in COVID funding and up to $22 million in enrolment-corridor and performance protection, subject to governance renewal and a long-term strategic plan, and the DIP refinancing was completed in January 2022. Enrolment had increased in 2020-21, driven partly by online growth, but later fell 14% in fall 2021, with further declines anticipated amid CCAA uncertainty.

KPMG LLP audited the amended and restated statements under Canadian accounting standards for not-for-profit organizations and issued an unmodified opinion, while highlighting a material uncertainty related to going concern and the extended CCAA stay. The report restated 2020 comparatives and amended the 2021 statements after identifying accounting and presentation errors, including endowment-allocation, vacation-pay, pension-benefit, deferred-contribution and interfund-transfer issues; the 2021 amendment reduced reported revenue to $193.4 million and increased the deficiency to $66.7 million without changing assets, liabilities, net assets or cash flows.

key_facts.fact: For fiscal 2020-21, Laurentian University reported total revenue of $193.4 million, total expenses of $260.1 million, a deficiency of revenue over expenses of $66.7 million, and total net assets of $15.4 million; the prior-year figures were $197.6 million, $200.9 million, $3.4 million, and $34.8 million respectively.

Laurentian reported available expendable resources of $85.9 million, compared with negative $19.8 million in the prior year; the report defines expendable net assets as internal reserves, internal endowments, and unrestricted net assets.
Laurentian reported 7,090 full-time-equivalent students in 2020-21, compared with 6,834 the previous year, and capital spending of $1.4 million compared with $2.8 million.

Laurentian reported a $14.0 million unfunded non-pension employee future-benefit obligation and no unfunded pension employee future-benefit obligation, compared with $10.3 million and negative $12.3 million respectively in the prior year.

Laurentian signed a 2020-25 Strategic Mandate Agreement with the Province in September 2020; the agreement reset the University's funding-corridor midpoint at 16,424 Weighted Grant Units and required enrolment to remain within plus or minus 3% of that midpoint beginning in fiscal 2020-21.
Laurentian said it decided to commence a proceeding under the Companies' Creditors Arrangement Act in the last quarter of fiscal 2020-21 after many years of recurring operating deficits.
On February 1, 2021, Laurentian obtained an order from the Ontario Superior Court of Justice Commercial List in its CCAA proceeding.
Ernst & Young Inc. was appointed monitor of Laurentian pursuant to an order of the CCAA Court.

On February 10, 2021, the CCAA Court approved a non-revolving, super-priority debtor-in-possession credit facility for Laurentian of up to $25.0 million to fund day-to-day operations and restructuring needs; the facility was increased to $35.0 million in May 2021.
At the end of April 2020, Laurentian's combined accumulated unrestricted-fund deficit and employee-benefit-liabilities deficit had reached $42.2 million.

Laurentian experienced a net enrolment decrease from fiscal 2015-16 through 2019-20 despite a $63.0 million campus-modernization program initiated in 2014; 2020-21 enrolment increased 3.7%, primarily through online-course growth, while new first-year enrolment declined 2.3%.
The Provincial Government required universities to reduce domestic tuition fees by 10% for 2019-20 and freeze domestic tuition fees for 2020-21.
As part of the CCAA process, Laurentian approved the closure of 39 English-language programs and 27 French-language programs and restructured the affected faculties and departments.

The CCAA claims procedure required non-employee creditors to identify and file claims against Laurentian by July 30, 2021, after which the Monitor or Court would determine the number and amount of accepted claims for potential compromise under a CCAA Plan.
Laurentian's restructuring initiatives included terminating its relationships with its federated universities: Thorneloe University, University of Sudbury, and Huntington University.
Laurentian said restructuring initiatives implemented to that point had reduced operating expenses by $40 million per year, a 25% reduction.

Although the report bears the fiscal-year-end date April 30, 2021, it states that its comprehensive real-estate review and its external review of Laurentian's Board of Governors, Senate, operational structure, systems, and processes were completed in January 2022.

The Canadian Architectural Certification Board granted the McEwen School of Architecture's professional Master of Architecture program initial accreditation for a term beginning July 1, 2021, making the school the 12th accredited architectural school in Canada.
Since 2016, Laurentian Online's headcount enrolment had increased by approximately 60%; it offered more than 19 bilingual or Indigenous-focused for-credit degree and certificate programs.

The Centre for Continuing Learning received Digital Capacity funding from eCampus Ontario, and Laurentian partnered with the Northern Policy Institute to launch a Sustainable Northern Economic Development micro-credential program.
Laurentian recognized $22.4 million in research grants and contracts in 2020-21, down from $24.2 million in the previous year.
Dr. Stefan Siemann received Canadian Foundation for Innovation funding for research using 3D imaging to identify cell-structure weaknesses in the SARS-CoV-2 virus.

Dr. Dave Pearson and six Indigenous organizations received Natural Resources Canada funding for a project on long-term, sustainable online climate-change adaptation capacity-building in First Nations communities.

With Heritage Canada funding, Dr. Joey-Lynn Wabie worked with Indigenous youth and residential-school survivors on the Tabik-gizis Kinamegewin project, producing videos about residential-school survivors' lives.

Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council funding supported training for 24 undergraduate students, while MITACS and industry partners supported 32 internships for graduate students and postdoctoral researchers and six undergraduate research-training awards.

Dr. Chantal Barriault received Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council funding and partnered with Science North on researcher science-communication training and a six-part Let's Talk COVID-19 seminar series.

Laurentian's fall 2020 student headcount was 9,323, up 4.2% from the previous year; spring/summer 2020 headcount increased 21% or 1,528 students, and online degree enrolment increased 26% or 435 students over fall 2019.

The report said Northern Ontario's student pool was projected to remain relatively flat while Toronto and the GTA were projected to grow, and that Laurentian subsequently experienced a 14% reduction in total fall 2021 enrolment; it also described preliminary estimates of another significant reduction in fall 2022 linked to CCAA uncertainty.

Laurentian's $66.7 million 2020-21 deficiency included $78.9 million of CCAA-related expenses, of which $70.1 million was included in liabilities subject to compromise; revenue was $193.4 million, while expenses excluding restructuring costs were $181.2 million.

Laurentian's 2020-21 revenue consisted primarily of $79.3 million in operating grants and contracts, $58.3 million in tuition fees, $22.4 million in research grants and contracts, $22.2 million in other fees and income, $5.6 million in sales and services, $5.6 million in amortization of deferred contributions, and no investment income.

Revenue was affected by the absence of a $4.3 million one-time Northern Sustainability grant received from the government in the prior year; pandemic-related sales and services revenue fell by $6.0 million and recognized research grants and contracts fell by $1.8 million, while tuition and fees increased by $5.1 million and other fees and income increased by $5.8 million.

Operating grants and contracts were $79.3 million, including $54.3 million in core operating and performance grants, $8.3 million in bilingualism grants, and $6.2 million in Northern grants; the remainder consisted of special-purpose grants.

Under SMA3, 25% of provincial funding was to be linked to performance metrics in 2020-21, rising to 35% in 2021-22 and 60% by 2024-25, but the Ministry of Colleges and Universities delayed activation of the performance-based grant for 2020-21 and 2021-22 because of COVID-19; Laurentian reported a full 2020-21 notional allocation of $16.2 million and a $21.6 million notional allocation for 2021-22.
Tuition and fees increased from $53.2 million in 2019-20 to $58.3 million in 2020-21; international-student tuition was $13.6 million, up 11.5%, while domestic tuition remained frozen.

Laurentian's recognized research revenue included expenditures of MIRARCO, a wholly controlled entity, and Laurentian's proportionate 20% share of the revenue and expenses of the Sudbury Neutrino Observatory Laboratory.

Laurentian recognizes research revenue when the related research expenditures occur; unspent research funding was reported as $18.6 million of deferred contributions at April 30, 2021, and part of that balance was potentially subject to compromise under a CCAA Plan.

The CCAA filing triggered defaults under Laurentian's seven interest-rate swap agreements; bank counterparties terminated the swaps and Laurentian recorded a $24.7 million loss on February 1, 2021.

Workforce restructuring and termination costs calculated under the Court-approved compensation-claim methodology totaled $44.7 million, while a further $0.7 million relating to the third-party Retirees' Health and Benefit Plan was included in liabilities subject to compromise.

Laurentian's historic federated relationships with Huntington University, University of Sudbury, and Thorneloe University were terminated through a statutory mechanism approved by the CCAA Court and upheld by the Court of Appeal; payments to the federated universities were $7.7 million in 2020-21.
Laurentian said the CCAA restructuring and other measures reduced annual expenses by approximately $40.0 million.

Laurentian had undertaken a $63.0 million campus modernization project and upgrades to the School of Education, student residences, and recreation centre; the projects were financed mostly by debt totaling $91.3 million as of February 1, 2021.

Laurentian invested $1.4 million in capital projects in 2020-21, primarily critical deferred-maintenance work funded by grants from the Ministry of Colleges and Universities Facility Renewal Program, while its deferred-maintenance backlog was estimated at $135.0 million.

Laurentian ended 2020-21 with $37.0 million in cash and short-term investments versus $3.4 million the previous year; the increase was attributed partly to a $25.0 million DIP facility secured with the CCAA filing, increased to $35 million in May 2021, and tighter spending controls.
Accounts receivable were $15.8 million, $11.3 million below 2019-20, which the report attributed to collections of major accounts.
Laurentian's $5.0 million unsecured Royal Bank line of credit and $26.0 million unsecured Desjardins line of credit were no longer available as of April 30, 2021.
Laurentian's investments totaled $62.2 million, up $8.2 million, and represented endowed funds whose income was restricted to donor-specified purposes.
Net investments in capital assets were $263.4 million versus $272.5 million in 2020; capital additions were $1.4 million compared with $2.8 million the previous year.

Laurentian reported deferred contributions of $36.4 million at April 30, 2021, compared with $37.4 million in 2020, and said a portion could be subject to compromise but the total could not yet be reasonably determined.

Laurentian reclassified $186.8 million of liabilities and claims as liabilities subject to compromise, including $11.3 million of accounts payable and accrued liabilities, $59.6 million of employee restructuring and termination costs, $1.3 million of short-term loans, $89.9 million of long-term debt, and $24.7 million of interest-rate-swap termination obligations.
Laurentian expected liabilities subject to compromise to be settled through a CCAA plan negotiated with creditors.

Laurentian reported long-term debt of $0 at April 30, 2021 versus $89.0 million in 2020, stating that the CCAA proceedings and resulting defaults made the debt immediately due and led to its reclassification as subject to compromise.

Effective April 2021, Laurentian amended the Retirement Plan of Laurentian University of Sudbury and its Federated and Affiliated Universities so future earnings would use a career-average formula, post-retirement indexation would be conditional, and employee contributions would match employer contributions.

An actuarial valuation produced a $9.5 million surplus in the Employees Retirement Plan, but Laurentian recorded a $9.5 million allowance for benefit reinstatement against it and recognized no pension-plan asset.

Obligations of $10.8 million under the Retirees' Health and Benefit Plan and $3.2 million under the Supplemental Retirement Plan were included in liabilities subject to compromise after both plans were terminated and their payments stayed during the CCAA proceedings.

Laurentian reported a $15.4 million deficiency in net assets at the end of 2020-21, which was $50.2 million below the previous year's restated net assets of $34.8 million; the deficiency of revenue over expenses was $66.7 million.
Laurentian restated prior-year net assets from $36.7 million to $34.8 million because of a $1.2 million correction of prior-period errors and a $0.7 million accounting-policy change.

Excluding CCAA effects and prior-period adjustments, Laurentian reported an adjusted excess of revenue over expenses of $12.2 million, including partial realization of CCAA-related cost savings in the last quarter of 2021.

Laurentian planned a real-estate review to identify assets that could be monetized, a review of Senate and Board of Governors governance and operations, and a new strategic plan developed with a third-party consultant at the Ministry of Colleges and Universities' request.

An Ontario support package included $35.0 million to refinance Laurentian's existing DIP financing, an intention to replace the DIP facility with a long-term loan after a successful CCAA plan, up to $6 million in COVID funding, and up to $22.0 million in enrolment-corridor and performance protection over several years.

As at April 30, 2021, Note 2 identified $186,820 thousand of obligations potentially subject to compromise and $79,137 thousand of restructuring costs connected with the CCAA proceedings.

The financial statements were prepared on a going-concern basis, but the CCAA proceedings, cash flows, net-assets deficiency and working-capital deficiency created material uncertainties casting significant doubt on the appropriateness of that assumption; continuation depended on restructuring and emergence from CCAA under a creditor-approved and court-approved plan.
key_facts.quote: The University's CCAA proceedings and circumstances relating to this event, including the University's cash flows, deficiency in net assets, and working capital deficiency, have resulted in material uncertainties that casts significant doubt about the appropriateness of the use of the going concern assumption.

key_facts.fact: The Province's loan agreement stated that the parties intended the $35 million DIP facility to be converted to a long-term loan when a CCAA plan was implemented, subject to terms agreed by Laurentian and the Province.

The government support was conditional on renewal of Laurentian's Board of Governors and completion of a long-term strategic plan; the first phase of Board renewal had commenced and the University was identifying a consultant to lead the strategic-plan process.
The first phase of renewal of Laurentian's Board of Governors commenced on December 16, 2021.

Mining Innovation Rehabilitation and Applied Research Corporation, or MIRARCO, is wholly controlled by Laurentian, whose sole voting membership gives it control; MIRARCO is consolidated in Laurentian's financial statements.
Sudbury Neutrino Observatory Laboratory, or SNOlab, is a not-for-profit partnership involving Laurentian and four other universities, and Laurentian recognizes 20% of SNOlab's revenue and expenses.

Northern Ontario School of Medicine and the Centre for Excellence in Mining and Innovation are disclosed as related parties but are not consolidated because Laurentian has no claim to their net assets and is not liable for their obligations.
Laurentian guaranteed a loan on behalf of the Laurentian University Student's General Association for construction of a student centre.
The consolidated financial statements were prepared under Canadian accounting standards for not-for-profit organizations, or ASNPO, and amounts are presented in thousands of Canadian dollars.

The University recognizes unrestricted contributions when received or receivable if they can be reasonably estimated and collection is reasonably assured; contributions restricted to future periods, operating purposes or capital assets are deferred and recognized as the related expenses or asset amortization occurs, while endowment contributions increase endowment net assets directly.

Tuition and ancillary fees, other fees and income, and sales and services are recognized in the fiscal period when the relevant courses, seminars, goods or services are provided; pledges are not recorded until received because they are not legally enforceable claims.
Investments are largely held in pooled funds and carried at fair value, with the University electing fair-value accounting for investments managed and evaluated on that basis.
Capital assets are amortized on a straight-line basis over estimated useful lives of 40 years for buildings, seven years for equipment and furnishings, and 15 years for site improvements.

Laurentian provided employee and post-retirement benefits through its Pension Plan, Retiree Health Benefit Plan and Supplementary Pension Plan, and made substantial changes to those plans in connection with the CCAA restructuring.
The most recent actuarial valuation of the Pension Plan was as of January 1, 2020; the next valuation was scheduled to be effective July 1, 2021.
Laurentian's interest-rate hedge was terminated during the year as a result of the CCAA proceedings.

Liabilities owing as of the February 1, 2021 CCAA filing date were stayed and subject to compromise under the anticipated plan, while obligations for goods and services provided after that date were excluded from liabilities subject to compromise.

Liabilities subject to compromise were subject to significant estimation uncertainty and could be materially adjusted because of the plan of arrangement, court action, disputed claims, proof-of-claim developments or other events.

The 2021 cash and investments note reported total cash and investments of $99,140 thousand, comprising $36,965 thousand of short-term cash and investments and $62,175 thousand of long-term investments; the 2020 restated comparative total was $57,389 thousand.

Laurentian maintained operating bank accounts totaling $28,363 thousand and three segregated accounts totaling $8,602 thousand; the segregated funds included $5,998 thousand of unspent research grants and awards, $2,492 thousand of other restricted funds and $112 thousand of employee and employer contributions to the Retiree Health Benefit Plan.
Accounts receivable totaled $15,793 thousand in 2021 after a $3,174 thousand allowance for doubtful accounts, compared with $27,214 thousand in 2020.

The University held $28,363,000 in operating bank accounts at April 30, 2021, compared with $2,637,000 in 2020, and $8,602,000 in three segregated accounts established in December 2020 for restricted funds.

The segregated accounts included $5,998,000 of unspent research grants and awards, $2,492,000 of other restricted funds, and $112,000 of employee and employer contributions to the Retiree Health Benefit Plan.
At April 30, 2021, accounts receivable totaled $18,967,000 before a $3,174,000 allowance for doubtful accounts, leaving $15,793,000 net receivables; $15,720,000 was current and $73,000 was long-term.

Effective April 2021, the Retirement Plan of Laurentian University of Sudbury changed members' transfer rights so that members reaching their early retirement date could no longer transfer a lump-sum value of their pension entitlement.

Effective July 1, 2021, the Pension Plan was renamed the Retirement Plan of Laurentian University of Sudbury and changed future-earnings calculations to a career-average basis, changed guaranteed post-retirement indexation to conditional indexation for future benefits, and modified employee contributions to match employer contributions.

The University stated that no future benefit improvements would be considered before July 1, 2025 unless the plan developed an excess surplus under pension regulations and the agreed terms, and recognized a $9,535,000 valuation allowance because it did not expect to realize those plan assets.

The term sheets agreed with the Laurentian University Faculty Association and LUSU provided for termination of the unfunded Retiree Health Benefit Plan on April 30, 2021; $10,757,000 of related liabilities was included in liabilities subject to compromise.

The University refunded $51,000 of employee contributions to the Retiree Health Benefit Plan, $5,000 of employer contributions from Sudbury Neutrino Observatory Laboratory and the Centre for Excellence in Mining and Innovation, and $4,000 of employer and employee contributions from the Federated Universities comprising Thorneloe University, University of Sudbury and Huntington University.

Under terms identified in the report as agreed with the Laurentian University Faculty Association and LUSA, payments from the unfunded Supplementary Pension Plan ceased on February 1, 2021; no further obligations were accrued for current or former non-union employees.
Liabilities of $3,216,000 relating to the Supplementary Pension Plan were included in liabilities subject to compromise at April 30, 2021.

Employee future-benefit remeasurements recognized directly in net assets totaled $9,298,000, comprising a $3,239,000 loss from the Retiree Health Benefit Plan curtailment, a $115,000 gain from the Supplementary Pension Plan curtailment, and a $12,422,000 gain from the Pension Plan amendment.

At April 30, 2021, employee-benefit obligations totaled $466,176,000, plan assets were $461,738,000, the Pension Plan showed $9,535,000 of assets before a matching benefit-reinstatement allowance, and accrued benefit liabilities of $13,973,000 were reclassified to liabilities subject to compromise.

The University's capital assets had a net book value of $263,385,000 at April 30, 2021, down from $272,531,000 in 2020, including buildings of $242,961,000, equipment and furnishings of $5,405,000, site improvements of $1,606,000 and land of $13,413,000.

The University reported $34,000 of buildings under construction and no equipment under construction at April 30, 2021, and determined that no impairment allowance for its integrated capital-asset group was required.
Government remittances payable, including payroll-related taxes, totaled $3,749,000 at April 30, 2021.

The University owed $1,324,000 under an unsecured short-term loan from TD Canada Trust bearing floating interest at 1.42%; the loan financed the Student Recreation Centre and was transferred to liabilities subject to compromise after the CCAA filing triggered an event of default.
On February 10, 2021, the Court approved a super-priority, non-revolving debtor-in-possession loan from Firm Capital Corporation of up to $25,000,000 to fund the University's day-to-day operations.

The DIP loan carried interest at the higher of 8.50% or the TD Canada Trust posted prime rate plus 6.05%; the University drew $10,000,000 on February 16, 2021 and $15,000,000 on March 26, 2021, paid $591,000 in debt-issuance costs and recognized $583,000 of interest expense.
On May 19, 2021, the DIP loan was amended to extend its repayment and maturity date to August 31, 2021 and increase the aggregate commitment to $35,000,000.
On August 20, 2021, the DIP loan was further amended to extend its repayment and maturity date to January 31, 2022.
The Ontario Government announced support through the Ministry of Colleges and Universities that included $35,000,000 to replace the existing DIP loan.

At April 30, 2021, the University's unsecured long-term debt totaled $89,927,000: Bank of Montreal $1,301,000; Royal Bank of Canada $12,881,000, $17,455,000, $2,555,000 and $38,640,000 across four loans; and TD Canada Trust $10,538,000 and $6,557,000 across two loans. The facilities financed residences, construction of the School of Education and Student Recreation Centre, and campus modernization projects.

The CCAA filing constituted an event of default under the long-term loan agreements, making the debt immediately due and payable; the University ceased accruing interest on the long-term debt and reclassified the obligations as liabilities subject to compromise from February 1, 2021.

The University's seven interest-rate swap counterparties terminated the swaps after the CCAA filing triggered contractual defaults, and the University recorded a $24,700,000 loss on termination in restructuring costs on February 1, 2021.

The Initial Order and subsequent amendments stayed payment of liabilities owing as of February 1, 2021 and placed those liabilities and additional creditor claims under a proposed plan of arrangement.
On May 31, 2021, the Court issued a Claims Process Order establishing procedures for determining claims and requiring creditors to submit claims to the Monitor.
On August 17, 2021, the Court issued an order establishing procedures for determining employee compensation claims.

Liabilities subject to compromise totaled $186,820,000 at April 30, 2021, comprising accounts payable and accrued liabilities of $11,301,000, employee future-benefit liabilities of $14,910,000, employee restructuring and termination costs of $44,658,000, the short-term loan of $1,324,000, long-term debt of $89,927,000 and the interest-rate swap termination obligation of $24,700,000.

Creditors asserted total claims of $360,291,000, but the University recognized only $186,820,000 as subject to compromise because it was still assessing the claims and could not estimate the amount subject to compromise; the report stated that future adjustments could be material.
Deferred contributions ended at $36,364,000 at April 30, 2021, consisting of $18,590,000 in research grants, $14,660,000 in other grants and trusts, and $3,114,000 in scholarships and bursaries.

During the year, the University recognized $21,061,000 of deferred contributions as revenue, including $15,168,000 of research income; related research expenses included $11,378,000 in salaries and benefits, $3,219,000 in operating and research costs, and $571,000 in scholarships and bursaries.

Of the $36,364,000 deferred-contributions balance, $4,390,000 was supported by cash held in separate bank accounts and $31,974,000 was not; the University said a portion could be subject to compromise but could not reasonably determine the total amount.
Deferred capital contributions totaled $128,268,000 at April 30, 2021, comprising $2,481,000 unspent and $125,787,000 unamortized contributions.

The University limited annual endowment distributions to 2.0% of the last 12 months' fair value of the endowment investment pool, down from 3.5% in 2020, and recognized a $590,000 administrative fee for managing the endowment during the year.
Net assets restricted for endowment totaled $61,482,000 at April 30, 2021, consisting of $49,998,000 in cumulative endowment contributions and $11,484,000 in cumulative reinvested investment income.

The endowment balance was $61.482 million at April 30, 2021, comprising cumulative endowment contributions of $49.998 million and cumulative reinvested investment income of $11.484 million, compared with a 2020 balance of $54.299 million.

Investment income was $8.232 million in 2021, consisting of a $357,000 unrealized loss, $2.842 million of interest income and $5.747 million of realized gains; $8.211 million related to the endowment and $21,000 to short-term investments.

The University reported $263.385 million of capital assets, financed in part by $91.251 million of liabilities subject to compromise, $23.317 million of internally financed capital projects and $125.787 million of unamortized deferred capital contributions, leaving $23.030 million as investment in capital assets.

The University internally financed $23.317 million of ongoing capital projects in 2021, using funds generated from ancillary operations, investment income or fundraising, compared with $27.250 million in 2020.

The University’s $5 million Royal Bank unsecured line of credit and $26 million Desjardins unsecured line of credit were no longer available at April 30, 2021; at April 30, 2020, it had drawn $14.4 million from the Desjardins facility and nothing from the Royal Bank facility.

The University guaranteed an $8.5 million Student General Association loan used to fund a new Student Centre, administered and collected the student levy used for repayment, and recorded no liability for the guarantee because no default event had occurred during the year.

The University disclosed uncertified class-action claims related to a data breach, employee claims, and CCAA claims involving construction-contractor delays and disputes and losses from disclaimed or terminated contracts; the outcomes were not determinable and the University said the asserted CCAA claims were material.
key_facts.quote: Claims asserted as part of these proceedings are material.

key_facts.fact: As part of the court-approved restructuring, the University reduced academic offerings, disclaimed federated-university arrangements, terminated or significantly reduced employee benefits, and reduced faculty and other staff.

The University recognized $78.904 million in restructuring costs, including $24.700 million for termination of interest-rate swaps, $44.658 million in employee restructuring and termination costs, and $70.097 million included in liabilities subject to compromise.
The University was the principal employer for the Pension Plan, which included the Federated Universities, SNOLAB, the Centre for Excellence in Mining and Innovation and MIRARCO.
Effective June 30, 2021, all Huntington University active employees ceased accruing further entitlement in the Pension Plan.

Active employees of the University of Sudbury and Thorneloe University who remained employed after December 31, 2021 were to become suspended members of the Pension Plan, while both universities remained employers with ongoing obligations to fund benefits earned by current and former employees.

Laurentian University and its unions agreed to establish a Joint Committee on the Benefits and Funding Policy and Long-Term Sustainability, with pension-plan improvements conditional on the plan meeting agreed funding levels.

Changes in non-cash working capital contributed $3.688 million to operating cash flows in 2021, including an $11.325 million increase from accounts receivable and a $6.384 million reduction from accounts payable and accrued liabilities.

Other fees and income totalled $22.161 million in 2021, including $7.101 million of scholarships, bursaries and other restricted contributions, $4.967 million of administrative fees and $2.647 million from sponsored students.

As a result of the CCAA proceedings, the University’s debt was stayed and in default, its interest-rate derivatives were terminated, and its remaining material interest-rate exposure at April 30, 2021 arose from a short-term variable-rate DIP loan.

On February 1, 2021, the University obtained an initial order protecting it from creditors under the CCAA; it subsequently pursued cost savings, restructuring and interim DIP financing, and reported that financial support from the Ontario Government was secured after year-end.

The University’s investment policy was approved by its Board of Governors, investments were managed by external investment managers, and investment performance was reviewed by the Board with assistance from the Finance Committee in monitoring investment and credit risks.

The University attributed reduced revenues in residences, food services and parking to the COVID-19 measures that followed the World Health Organization’s March 2020 pandemic declaration and the closure of physical premises at postsecondary institutions.

After resuming in-person teaching and research in fall 2021, the University returned to remote course delivery during the Omicron wave and began a staged return to campus on February 7, 2022, prioritizing experiential learning.

NOSM was a related party of the University; Laurentian and Lakehead University were its only voting members, the University had no claim to NOSM’s operating net assets and no liability for its obligations, and NOSM occupied and leased campus buildings for a nominal amount.

The Ministry of Colleges and Universities introduced proposed legislation on April 15, 2021 to establish NOSM as an independent, standalone degree-granting institution; the legislation was still pending customary approvals.

During 2021, the University recorded $939,000 in recoveries and charges for goods and services with NOSM; at April 30, 2021 it reported $393,000 receivable from NOSM and $1.412 million of stayed payables to NOSM.

CEMI was created on April 23, 2007 to advance study, research and innovation, and the University contributed $10 million received from the Provincial Government to create and fund it; the University had no claim to CEMI’s assets and no liability for its obligations.
During 2021, the University recorded $575,000 in recoveries and charges for goods and services with CEMI; at April 30, 2021 it reported no receivable from CEMI and a $7,000 payable to CEMI.
The University had an economic interest in its student associations because it collected student fees on their behalf and recorded transactions with them at agreed exchange amounts.

The University changed accounting policies and financial-statement presentation during fiscal 2021 and, in reviewing its accounts for the CCAA process, identified items that had not been properly recognized, measured or presented in prior-period statements.
The University retrospectively reclassified $37.423 million of deferred contributions from non-current to current liabilities, with no change to total liabilities.
The University discontinued a reserve account for future endowment spending and retrospectively transferred its 2020 debit balance of $673,000 from deferred contributions to endowment net assets.

The University retrospectively reclassified accrued vacation for staff, senior management and administrative professionals from employee future benefits net assets to unrestricted net assets, increasing ending unrestricted net assets by $1.847 million and opening unrestricted net assets by $1.799 million.

The University found that it had not accrued each year for payments to the Financial Services Regulatory Authority of Ontario for the Pension Benefit Guarantee Fund; it corrected the 2020 comparative statements by increasing accounts payable and accrued liabilities by $702,000 and salaries and benefits expense by $214,000.

The University identified an error that understated accrued vacation pay for staff, administrative employees and senior management by $747,000 and corrected the comparative statements by increasing salaries and benefits expense by $81,000.

An in-depth review of the University’s endowments over the prior 17 years identified errors in allocating investment earnings and distributing endowment funds, resulting in a reported understatement of endowment net assets of $1.454 million, compared with $1.981 million for 2019.
key_facts.quote: The University performed an in-depth analysis of its endowments for the prior 17 years which identified errors in the allocation of investment earnings to endowment funds and in the distribution of amounts from endowments in prior years.

key_facts.fact: The University reclassified $1.119 million of endowment investments from cash and short-term investments to investments in the 2020 comparative statements.

The University corrected its 2020 statements after determining that contributions received for the Retiree Health Benefit Plan had been recorded as operating cash and deferred contributions rather than employee future benefits liabilities, increasing employee future benefits liabilities by $1.769 million.

The University corrected a $264,000 capital-project cost that had been expensed instead of capitalized, increasing capital assets and investment-in-capital-assets net assets by that amount and reducing operating and research expense.

After restatements and corrections, the 2020 comparative statements reported total assets of $358.784 million, total liabilities of $323.960 million, total net assets of $34.824 million, revenue of $197.554 million, expenses of $200.941 million and a deficiency of revenue over expenses of $3.387 million.

For the year ended April 30, 2020, the comparative consolidated statement of operations was restated: revenue decreased from $198,397 thousand to $197,554 thousand, expenses decreased from $201,517 thousand to $200,941 thousand, and the deficiency of revenue over expenses increased from $3,120 thousand to $3,387 thousand.

The 2020 comparative corrections decreased other fees and income by $843 thousand, increased salaries and benefits expense by $295 thousand and operating and research expense by $130 thousand, and eliminated a $1,001-thousand investment loss.

The University's total net assets for 2020 were restated from $36,682 thousand to $34,824 thousand; the restated balances included unrestricted deficiency of $23,640 thousand, employee future benefits deficiency of $22,557 thousand, internally restricted net assets of $3,848 thousand, investment in capital assets of $22,874 thousand, and endowment of $54,299 thousand.

The restated 2020 cash-flow statement reported $1,877 thousand from operating activities, $(1,011) thousand from financing activities, $(2,626) thousand from investing activities, a net decrease of $1,760 thousand in cash and short-term investments, and year-end cash and short-term investments of $3,425 thousand.

Because of ongoing financial and operational difficulties, the University applied for an initial order under the Companies' Creditors Arrangement Act; the requested relief included a stay of proceedings and appointment of a monitor, and the notes state that the stay had been extended.
The Court approved interim financing for the University on February 10, 2021, with a maturity date of January 31, 2022.
The DIP Loan amount was increased from $25,000 thousand to $35,000 thousand on May 19, 2021.
The DIP Loan repayment and maturity date were extended to January 31, 2022, on August 20, 2021.
The University drew the additional $10,000 thousand under the DIP Loan on August 24, 2021 and incurred a $550-thousand amendment fee.
The Ontario Government announced a support package through the Ministry of Colleges and Universities for the University on December 16, 2021.

On January 19, 2022, the University and the Ministry of Colleges and Universities executed a Replacement DIP Facility to replace the existing DIP Loan, with proceeds to be used to repay the existing DIP Loan in full.
The Court authorized the University on January 27, 2022 to borrow under the Replacement DIP Facility for up to $35,000 thousand.
At the January 28, 2022 advance under the Replacement DIP Facility, the interest rate was 1.11 percent.

The Replacement DIP Facility terms stated that the parties intended to convert it to a long-term loan when a CCAA plan was implemented, on terms to be agreed by the University and the Ministry of Colleges and Universities.
key_facts.quote: the intention of the parties for the DIP Facility to be converted to a long-term loan on the implementation of a CCAA Plan, upon such terms and conditions as may be agreed by the [University] and [MCU] prior to that time

key_facts.fact: The Government support package included up to $6,000 thousand in COVID-19 relief funding and enrolment-corridor and performance protection of up to $22,000 thousand over several years, subject to agreed terms and conditions including renewal of the Board of Governors and completion of a long-term strategic plan.

The first phase of renewal of the University's Board of Governors commenced on December 16, 2021, while the process of identifying a consultant for the University's long-term strategic plan was still in progress.
The original financial statements had an auditor's report dated March 7, 2022.

The financial statements were amended after issuance because the University's continuing CCAA-related account analysis identified errors involving elimination of interfund transfers between unrestricted and internally restricted net assets and accounting for termination of the Retiree Health Benefit Plan.
key_facts.quote: The financial statements that were original issued with an auditors' report date of March 7, 2022 have been amended for errors identified after their issuance.

key_facts.fact: The 2021 restatement decreased other fees and income revenue by $2,138 thousand, decreased salaries and benefits expense by $141 thousand, operating and research expense by $1,075 thousand, and restructuring costs by $233 thousand, and increased employee future benefits remeasurements and other items by $689 thousand.

As restated for 2021, revenue was $193,396 thousand rather than $195,534 thousand, expenses were $260,067 thousand rather than $261,516 thousand, and the deficiency of revenue over expenses was $66,671 thousand rather than $65,982 thousand.
The 2021 amendments did not affect reported assets, liabilities, net assets on the statement of financial position, or cash flows; disclosures in notes 6, 12, 13, 20 and 21 were revised.

In the 2021 statement of changes in net assets, the deficiency of revenue over expenses was restated from $(65,982) thousand to $(66,671) thousand and employee future benefits remeasurements and other items from $8,609 thousand to $9,298 thousand, leaving the total deficiency of revenue over expenses unchanged at $(15,366) thousand.
